utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, General. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Barney Thomas, Bronagh McKenna --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: -- Dan Saxon, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thomas. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all the participants in this case. Mr. Perisic will be presented today by Novak Lukic and Boris Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning. Just to remind you once again that you're bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Lukic. I see I'm being called Judge David in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Lukic. Once I said yes, Mr. Lukic, then it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, once again good morning. Now I will try to stick to my word I gave you yesterday so we will try to be as quick as possible so that you can return to your family today.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I would like to ask some questions that follow from the questions and your answers provided to Mr. Thomas. I will try to clarify certain things. On Monday he asked several questions regarding the military budget, and the portions of the military budget going for the MOD or the army, respectively. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He also put it to you that from that pie, so to say, called the military budget, some 95 per cent went for the Army of Yugoslavia and 5 per cent for the MOD. And you said that the ratio was probably 85 per cent for the army and 15 per cent for the MOD. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He also put it to you that once the military budget or the portion for the Yugoslav Army was approved on a daily basis, it was allocated through the accounting centre. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. It's not the accounting centre of the army. It is the accounting centre of the MOD.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what I wanted to clarify first of all. So the part of the military budget allocated for the army, how was that disbursed? How was that distributed, so to say, in plain language?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, this is a technical issue, the distribution of the funding where it is kept and so on, but we are here talking about the accounting per se. If you allow me to remind you of what we talked about earlier, the accounting and budgeting administration of the Federal Ministry of Defence, which is an independent administration directly responsible to the Federal Minister of Defence, has as one of its main tasks to prepare the rules on financial business of all the units in the army and in the MOD, but now we are talking about the methodology and ways in which monies were distributed. So in order not to go into these technical issues, whether it was a pie, as you say, or whether it was done in another way, it all depended on whoever was competent for a particular task, for the execution of a particular task. And please allow me just to remind you of yet another thing that we need to clarify. The role of these two administrations, so I'm talking about the administration for systemic and status-related issues. According to the Article 85 of the relevant regulation, this particular administration is mentioned as the administration in charge of monitoring the payments of salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will come to that in a second. Hold on. We will look at certain documents, and I will ask you to comment, but let us take it step-by-step. When asked by Mr. Thomas, you also said that when we are talking about the portion of the military budget going for the army, approximately 65 per cent went for salaries and pensions. So my question is as follows: Did the Army of Yugoslavia have anything to do with the distribution of pensions?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, one additional explanation. The only institution responsible for pensions was the fund, so-called SOVO. This was the acronym, and we used it. This was the fund that was in charge of calculating and distributing pensions. The General Staff of the Yugoslav Army had nothing to do with the pensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us approximately of these 65 per cent of the military budget that went for pensions and salaries, what was the portion that went for pensions approximately?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the number of pensioners and the number of active members of the military service, it was approximately 40 per cent for pensions and the remaining amount for active servicemen, but this is very approximate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what I asked you. Also, Mr. Thomas put it to you on the same day that the VJ controlled war reserves. My question is as follows: To which particular body was the directorate for war reserves subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was directly subordinated to the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was its main task?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Its main task is clear from the very name of this directorate. So it had to provide funding, which was also visible in the budget, and if requested by the General Staff and the ministry, it had to provide different reserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the Exhibit P756 on the screen. These are minutes from the 25th session of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I do not have a paper version, but I believe it will be legible enough, and if necessary, I can read it out for you.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So as I said, this is page 1 of these minutes. The session was held on 30th of August, 1994, and if we can now see page 3 in B/C/H. I believe it's also page 3 in English. I need conclusion number 7. So this is at the very end of this document in both language versions, at the last page.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only see item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hold on just a second. We will wait for the English version as well. So as I said, item number 7. So, General Nikolic, these are the conclusions adopted by the Supreme Defence Council following this session. In item 7, we can read as follows: "In order to maintain the requisite level of combat readiness of the Army of Yugoslavia, it is essential within the limitations of the funds approved by the federal budget, to secure a more regular and steady flow on funds for the army and an additional 35.5 million dinars. The salaries of members of the Yugoslav Army shall be regularly harmonised with those in other sectors of the society." And the following paragraph reads as follows: "The federal ministry of defence shall regularly inform the Supreme Defence Council at its sessions about the implementation of this task." It follows from this document -- can you tell us, Mr. Simic [sic], what follows from this document? Who was in charge of salaries for members of the army?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the last sentence clearly says that the Federal Ministry of Defence shall be responsible for providing money for the salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we are in a private session, could we please have a look at the document P749. This is also a document that is under seal. These are minutes from the 36th session of the Supreme Defence Council. This is it. On the screen we can see the minutes from the 36th session of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 12th of May, 1995. Could we please take a look at page 5 in B/C/H. I would like to see conclusion number 5. I believe it is also page 5 in English. So item number 5. That's the one. Can we just see it in English as well. It is probably on the previous page in English. I apologise. Once again, this is a conclusion of the Supreme Defence Council, and it reads as follows: "Secure a regular inflow of funds. The federal government shall take care of this matter not later than in the course of next week. As a part of this, secure funds for the payment of salaries to members of the Army of Yugoslavia." How do you read this conclusion of the Supreme Defence Council, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 5 of these conclusions of the Supreme Defence Council clearly says that it is a duty of the federal government, as the only authorised body to do this, to secure the necessary funds for the payment of salaries to members of the Army of Yugoslavia not later than in the course of the following week, and this conclusion is very clear. It is only the federal government that can do it pursuant to its authorities stipulated by legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we are still in a private session, we will move to a different topic, but this is yet another document that is under seal. Mr. Thomas asked you, and you said both in direct examination and during the cross-examination, when we are talking about the period in which the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had sanctions against the Republic of Serbia, that members of the families who stayed in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had very dire problems. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you confirmed to Mr. Thomas that these families had really hard times. So do you just remember that this is what you said?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was just waiting for the interpretation to be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So could we please look at the document that we saw previously, P756. So again this -- these are the minutes from the 25th session of the Supreme Defence Council, and the session was held on 30th of August, 1994. I need conclusion number 5 this time. Page 3 in the B/C/S as well, if possible. The meeting was held on the 30th of August, 1994. That is beyond dispute. That's after the federal government adopted that decision on the introduction of sanctions. Conclusion number 5: "Military officers currently in Republika Srpska but disagreeing with the policies of Republika Srpska's leadership and asking to go back, shall be welcomed back to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." Have you read that, sir? My question is --

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Nikolic, do you know the members of the VRS who were handled by the 30th Personnel Centre in fact accepted this invitation by the FRY's leadership, or did they, in fact, remain in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the Republic of Serbian Krajina or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is in reference to members of the VRS when the -- the FRY imposed its sanctions on Republika Srpska. That is when the Contact Group plan had been refused in early August.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any officers, and if so how many, of the VRS in fact went back to the FRY at the invitation of the Supreme Defence Council as the document states?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I say something else. We actually conducted analysis and not a single member of the VRS in fact went back to the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that we don't have any LiveNote, at least not on my screen. I have no problem pressing ahead though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. There -- I don't know how to call these things, but on the screen on the left you do have LiveNote. You can get LiveNote. And -- okay. This is a problem we all have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The important thing is the actual proceedings are recorded. As soon as that is the case, we might as well continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, had those officers returned to the VJ, would they have been receiving salaries throughout that period from the FRY and the army? Had they responded to the invitation by the FRY.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I think: If they'd gone back, they would have had to receive some salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go back into open session, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to bring up another subject, something that actually follows from one of your earlier answers. P1864. That's what I think the number is. It's a document by the 3rd Army following the talks with Chief Perisic about certain officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1865. It appears that I made a mistake. P1865. [In English] P1865. [Interpretation] There, now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I'm not sure if you remember this document. Hold on a minute, sir.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The print's too small. I can't see a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then I'll try to jog your memory, General. It's a list of officers following the talks with General Perisic, those handled by the 40th Personnel Centre in the SVK and also a list of those officers who expressed their desire to retire.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just take it easy, please. One step at a time. Mr. Thomas put it to you based on this document that the officers not wishing to be handled by the 40th Personnel Centre and then go to the SVK chose as their only other option to retire. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under the Law on the VJ, does a person being sent to a unit have the right to appeal that decision?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person being sent or transferred, and this is something that the Law on Promotions also clearly states, has no right to appeal a decision like that. The person must comply. If that is what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first -- the first question is: Does this person have the right to appeal?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the person does have the right to appeal. This is the Law on General Administrative Procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Any person at all, for example, gets a secondment or an order to transfer. Does that person have the right to appeal that order?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the appeal stay the actual execution?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know from the period when you came to the personnel administration and had under you the 30th Personnel Centre -- so, do you perhaps know that any person who was sent like that through the 30th or 40 Personnel Centres ever lodged an appeal about an action like this?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a small correction. When I came there, there was only a 30th Personnel Centre. The 40th was no longer around. Based on my experience, based on my knowledge and any information that I may have had at the time, there wasn't a single person who did that at the time. Quite the contrary, in fact. All of the persons of their own free will signed these statements to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down. The interpreter is having difficulty. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. It won't happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question still covering the same subject, and I mean officers now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can counsel reframe the question. The interpreter did not understand the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about any active-duty servicemen? There is a decision that is taken on the termination of his service and for that person to be retired. Would a person not have the right to appeal that decision?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that person has the right to appeal this decision before the Supreme Court, and this is actually included in the legal remedies. Any order can be appealed like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Court, that is a civilian court, not a military court; right?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The supreme military court dealing with matters to do with administrative aspects in terms of regulating these appeals, ruling on them and so on and so forth. As far as criminal matters were concerned, well, one knows how that is handled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on to another subject. Actually this is my third subject, something that was brought up by Mr. Thomas. He was using certain documents as he was examining you about this. It was about the execution of actual disciplinary decisions adopted by courts in the VRS. Let me first bring back Prosecution Exhibit P2420.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, your microphone is off. You will have to start all over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we have before us a sentence by the military disciplinary court, that attached to the air force and anti-aircraft defence of the VRS. The date is the 20th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor wanted to know about person number 2, the second accused Nedeljko Vujic, holding the rank of major, military post 7272, Banja Luka. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you look at the disposition that is included in this judgement, it reads: "Found guilty Nedeljko Vujic --"

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please zoom in on the part that says, "Found guilty." And then the paragraph just under that heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It reads that the --

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've lost the image on the screen. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me read that portion for you. It says in relation to Vujic, right down the middle: "Accused number 2, Nedeljko Vujic, on the 29th of May, 1993, was not authorised to leave his service."

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is the day Major Nedeljko Vujic left his unit. That's the date; right?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please pull the document up a little to see the heading. Yes, like that. Thank you. Can we please pull the English up as well so the Chamber may see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The sentence takes effect on the 8th of October, 1995. That's what it says, doesn't it? It's the clause on entry into force; right?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's in the upper right corner where you can see the stamp.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I do see that now. Yes, yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just find out. There are two dates there. There's the 8th of October, 1995. There's the 20th of September, 1995. How do we determine that it takes effect on the 8th of October, 1995? I don't know what those two dates mean, and could the witness explain them to us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Indeed, General. As a lawyer, can you explain what the date means when the sentence is due to take effect and what is the difference between these two dates?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you look at the heading where it is stated who adopted this decision, it says that it was passed on the 20th of September, 1995. And then on the right-hand side we can see the two stamps on the same page. You can see that the sentence takes effect on the 8th of October, 1995, and then there's a portion that I can't see. The 8th of October, 1995, and then the Chamber president signed this. Entry into force, what does that mean. That means that all the deadlines have now passed for any legal remedies or appeals to be lodged and the decision must be executed. That's what it means if you ask me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is about a month of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to another document. May I just ask you to remember about this person, Nedeljko Vujic. The sentence says that he committed this crime on the 20th of May, 1993, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the last part of counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last part of counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will have to slow down. It says that Nedeljko Vujic left the unit, committed the crime on the 20th of May, 1993, and the sentence was passed on the 20th of September, 1995. Now I would like to see another document that you saw previously, Mr. Nikolic, in relation to the same person, but I believe that we need to move into a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's P4241. I'm not sure whether this document is under seal. No, it doesn't seem to be, so we can remain in an open session. So P4241.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, we don't have that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. P2421.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you saw the document that is issued by the command of the air force and the anti-aircraft defence which was sent to the personnel administration of the General Staff in relation to the judgement that we saw previously. So what do we see here? I will read it out for you, General. First of all, we can see that this document signed by General Velickovic is dated 29th of January, 1996. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Item 1 here mentions Nedeljko Vujic, lieutenant-colonel. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the previous document he was a major, and here we can see that three years later now he was lieutenant-colonel. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down to see another portion that Mr. Thomas already showed you, and it relates to Mr. Vujic. It says the officer mentioned under item 1 --

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to read, but I can hear what you are reading out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "The officers under numbers 1 and 4 have been in service in the VJ for two or more years. They have achieved very good and excellent results, and a possible confirmation of this measure would be a pure loss for the air force and anti-air defence of the Army of Yugoslavia." This is what Velickovic says in this document. And now please let us look at yet another document that you saw previously, and this is P2422. This is a document on the termination of his professional military service issued by the command of the air force PVO of the Army of Yugoslavia. The date here is the 13th of October, 2005, and we can see that he will retire with the rank of colonel. Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Question number 1: Mr. Nedeljko Vujic, from the moment when he left his unit in the Army of Republika Srpska in 1993 as a major until the moment when he's retired, has he been promoted within the Army of Yugoslavia? Could you see this in these documents?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from everything you read out, I can see that he was promoted and he was still in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this document, could you draw a conclusion as to what he did once he left the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of these documents, we can see that he went back to his original unit. So he went back to the command of the air force and PVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So on the basis of these documents, can you conclude whether the Army of Yugoslavia respected the decision of the military court of Republika Srpska or not?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, because these were two separate systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we will see the second example that Mr. Thomas put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give each other a chance as you speak so that the interpretation can take place. Don't overlap quickly. And try to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I'm not sure whether P2417 is a document that is under seal or not. If not, could we please look at document P2417.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a judgement regarding the second person. His name was Zoran Antic, and you discussed this example with Mr. Thomas as well. We will enlarge this, and I will read out similar data. So the judgement was issued on 23rd of September, 1995, by the military disciplinary court of the command of the air force and PVO, and the Prosecutor was interested in the person named under item 2, Mr. Zoran Antic. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here we can see that his current whereabouts were unknown, that he was in Srb, and that he was in the VRS since 15th of February, 1993. Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So here we can see the text of the judgement and it says that these were active military servicemen who left the service on their own will, and Antic, Zoran, left the service on 13th of March, 1993 [as interpreted], and never returned. Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the disciplinary punishment was pronounced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Just a correction in the transcript, sir, and it may be a translation error. I'm not certain, but at page 18, line 24, my learned friend referred to the date upon which Zoran Antic left his unit as being the 13th of March, 1993, but I see from the document that's on the screen, at least the English version, that it's 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks very much. The transcript will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thomas. You're absolutely correct. So this was the 13th of March, 1995. Could we now look at the following document: P2419. [In English] 2419.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now this is an order of the chief of the personnel administration of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, issued on the 5th of February, 1996, which concludes that the professional military service of Zoran Antic has been terminated. At the very end of the document we can see legal remedies, and it says: "This order is final and an appeal may not be filed against it, but an administrative action may be instituted at the Supreme Military Court in Belgrade ..." This is what it says?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in the previous cases we -- case we had an example of a person who returned to his unit in the VJ. On the basis of this document, can you conclude whether this particular person went back to his unit in the VJ or not?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see this explanation, and in this explanation it is indicated that on the basis of the attached documents it can be concluded that he did not return to his unit to explain his absence from his unit, and therefore he does not deserve any payment. So he did not return to his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it in the interest of the Army of Yugoslavia to pay any money to persons who did not go back to their units in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no grounds on the basis of which they could be paid, but also there was a legal basis for this based in Article 107, paragraph 1 on the Law on the Army. So they could not be paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was very specific. Was it in the interest of the Yugoslav Army to pay persons who did not belong to their units?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it in the interest of Yugoslavia to keep such persons into their -- into its records as if they were their members?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such persons were erased from all the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Could we now please have a look at the document P2413. This is a different topic that was raised by Mr. Thomas, and it had to do with initiating disciplinary proceedings against persons who came to the Serbian Army of Krajina through the 40th Personnel Centre. We will now see this document. This is an order signed by General Perisic on 9th of November, 1995, and in your answer to Mr. Thomas you talked about the contents of the document. My first question is: Do you know whether in November of 1995 the Republic of Serbian Krajina existed at all?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In November of 1995, was there a Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no army and no Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please move into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the document P0 -- 708 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we can see on the screen, these are the minutes of the 43rd session of the Supreme Defence Council of the FRY held on the 29th of August, 1995. Could we please see the following page. I'm interested in conclusion number 2. Conclusion 2 says that: "Disciplinary or criminal proceedings shall be initiated against professional members of the 40th Personnel Centre for whom there are grounds to believe that they have committed a violation of discipline or a criminal offence." This is a conclusion of the Supreme Defence Council. We saw the date. It was in August. So was this binding for the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, General, I believe you mentioned this in your answer to Mr. Thomas, whether after the Operation Storm and after many people went to the territory of the FRY that certain members of the Serbian Army of Krajina requested to come back to the military service and to be posted at particular posts within the army?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before they were appointed to certain duties, did such person need to be checked? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, were there military disciplinary courts and military disciplinary jurisdiction in Krajina after the Storm?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment Krajina disappeared, all the military disciplinary bodies and all other institutions disappeared as well. So there were no more military disciplinary courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go back into an open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm about to move on to my last set of questions stemming from Mr. Thomas's questions. He showed you several articles of the Law on the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to P197, specifically Article 16. Page 2 in the B/C/S and page 5 in the English. Can we zoom in, please, on Article 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 reads as follows: "Generals and commanding officers performing duties for which the rank of general has been determined in the establishment shall be appointed to positions by the president of the republic. Other officers, non-commissioned officers and soldiers shall be appointed to positions in the army by the Chief of the General Staff or a commanding officer authorised by him, and in the Federal Ministry of Defence by the federal minister of defence or a commanding officer authorised by him." Sir, when they talk about being appointed to positions, what exactly does that mean?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Being appointed to positions means that persons are sent to a particular unit. A person is then appointed to an establishment post by his own superior officer. His service situation is then determined, what is his duty, what is his position, and so on and so forth, any other elements affecting that person's salary under the terms of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we look at this article, it was the defence minister who appointed you when your term began with the defence ministry; right?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He appointed me. And may I add something? The officer in charge of both appointing a person to a general -- to a particular position and generally the -- making an appointment writes up an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of that in the SVK and the VRS for as long as the two armies were around?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a person was sent to serve with those armies, the service situation would be dealt with by the appropriate officers under the regulations of the VRS and the SVK, respectively. They were now at all practical intents outside the chain of command of the VJ and were part of the chain of command of these other armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown Article 8 of the Law on the VJ by both myself and the Prosecutor, and you said something about paragraph 2 of that article talking about the term "service" and what is considered as service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to Article 10 of that same law, which should be on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This article defines what is defined as service relations. It has been shown a number of times, therefore, I will not be reading it out loud. For as long as those officers were in the VRS, who did they have service relations to, the VRS and the SVK?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had service relations to their superiors in the VRS and the SVK alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now move on to Article 171, another article that Mr. Thomas discussed with you. Rather, 177 and 178. Those are the two that I'm interested in. B/C/S reference is page 15, and the English reference is page 45. This was shown to you by Mr. Thomas. You should have it in front of you, sir. Mr. Thomas showed you how the law defines various military courts, the first instance and then the higher military disciplinary court. 177 -- 178 states that they'll be established at the General Staff under the [indiscernible] of the army, air force and anti-aircraft defence as well as the navy. The high military disciplinary court shall be attached to the General Staff. It's actually quite specific. It is specifically envisaged by the law; right?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This may sound like too easy a question because we were looking at those documents. What about the VRS and the SVK? Do they have their own military disciplinary courts?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on what regulations?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on the Army of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, same thing. The Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes my re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Nikolic, thank you so much, that brings us to the end of your testimony. We thank you very much for taking the time to come and testify at the Tribunal. You are now excused. You may go home. Please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I keep you a minute or two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, go ahead. As long as you don't say anything that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It won't take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing at all, really. I just wish to thank you. You, the OTP, and the Defence for giving me an opportunity to appear in this courtroom in order to tell the truth and nothing but the truth. Another thanks goes to you, Your Honours, because you had to reorganise the entire schedule for this day in order to meet the requirements I expressed yesterday. I do wish to thank you yet again for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. Once again, travel well back home. You are excused. You are -- you are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just greet the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Just stand down, Mr. Nikolic. They will greet you in due course just now. You are now excused. You may stand down. We are still in court. You can't do your greetings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do have a witness lined up. I do want to ask myself to exchange greetings with Mr. Nikolic. Therefore, I think this might be a good opportunity for that if we take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We will take a break and come back at quarter to. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is ready for our next witness, Mr. Gajic, Branko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may be seated, sir, and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please introduce yourself for the record.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, you testified previously in two trials before this Tribunal, and you know about the kind of problem we normally encounter when both persons speak the same language during an examination. Therefore, I would like to ask you to pause each time before you start answering a question. I'll also do my best to make a pause after each of your answers to give the interpreters a chance to accurately interpret the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that I've mentioned this, can you specify the trials in which you've testified and on whose behalf you appeared.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have appeared twice. The first time was in the Milutinovic, Sainovic, Ojdanic, Pavkovic et al. trial, and I appeared as an Ojdanic Defence witness. I also testified in the case against Ramush Haradinaj as an OTP witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I will read back to you portions from your CV which I believe are relevant. Please specify if the information is correct -- rather, confirm that the information is correct.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were born in 1946; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You completed the Belgrade Military Academy in 1967, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Up until 1972, you were engaged on what they term "troop activities"; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Between 1972 and your retirement, you worked with the security bodies of the JNA and later the VJ; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your first period there you were with the Guards Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, you had completed your education with the military staff academy in 1978, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, the General Staff School of the German Bundeswehr in Hamburg in 1981; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Up until 1986, you worked as a clerk in the SSNO's security administration; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were then chief of security in a division stationed in Osijek, Croatia, between 1986 and 1988; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And after that, up until October 1990, you worked as chief of security in the Tuzla Corps in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1990, you completed the war academy, which was later renamed the National Defence School, which was the highest body of military education in Yugoslavia at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Between 1990 and 1992, you worked with the security administration as assistant chief and then later chief of the first department.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Between 1992 and April 1994, you worked as chief of the security sector of the 1st Army of the VJ; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Between 1994 and the 31st of December, 2002, you were back with the security administration as chief of the counter-intelligence department. You also worked as assistant chief and deputy chief of the security administration, and you continued in that position until April 1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't 2001 -- it wasn't 2002, rather. It was 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. You were, in fact, pensioned off on the 31st of December, 2001; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Over that last period you worked as assistant chief of the security administration, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You retired as a general -- major general.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were, in fact, born in the Republic of Croatia, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, could we first discuss what it is exactly that security bodies do, and what is the difference between their remit and that of intelligence bodies, just to put the Trial Chamber in the picture. What exactly do security bodies in an army do?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the fundamental tasks and obligations of security bodies, in the VJ at least, were counter-intelligence protection of the VJ and the country's defence from any activities by foreign intelligence and counter-intelligence services, from terrorist organisations and crime groups. The main task of a military intelligence administration breaks down as follows: They organise a gathering of intelligence and information abroad and not domestically in order to identify any indicators of a possible aggression against the FRY. Conditionally speaking, the security administration might be defined as a defensive service; and the intelligence administration is, in a manner of speaking, an offensive service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned counter-intelligence activity and said that this was something for the security bodies. Can you please explain that term? What is it called that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, the concept itself suggests an answer. "Counter" means "against." An army faces a threat. Perhaps the army itself, perhaps a threat from abroad, and then we use some measures peculiar to our work and technology peculiar to our work in order to ward off these threats. That is what we call counter-intelligence activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think this applies to both the JNA and the VJ. What were the relations between the security bodies and the intelligence bodies?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: There was co-operation, and there was a mutual exchange of intelligence and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What sort of information were you sending their way, and what sort of information were they sending your way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we in the military intelligence administration were providing any information that were relevant in terms of the foreign element. We monitored this foreign element as a potential threat to Yugoslavia's security, whereas they provided to us information that had to do with protecting the VJ as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the term stated on page 31, word 22, where it says security organs as military intelligence administration is not good. I think we should be using "security administration," what the security organs are doing, since we'll be using these terms quite frequently. I hope the interpreters agree with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please give me an example just for the sake of Their Honours. What were you focused at? What were you interested in? What was it that you protected, and what was it that the intelligence administration focused on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we protected -- let me give you an example. For example, specific plans of preparation and engagement of the Army of Yugoslavia, so war plans. Furthermore, we protected individuals, officers who were at high positions which were very sensitive positions since they -- they were aware of very many sensitive military information. So we protected military information. Furthermore, we protected weapons and equipment which were often subject of attacks or theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And intelligence bodies. You mentioned war plans, for example. What would it be that the intelligence organs would be interested in? Whose war plans?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Intelligence organs were interested in plans of potential aggressors against Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now take a look at some documents concerning what we've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to comment -- I would like this witness to comment on the rules of the security military bodies. Document is D89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before he does that, at page 32, lines 21 to 22, the witness says: "Intelligence organs were interested in plans of potential aggressors against Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." From what -- how he described the security and the intelligence organs, it seems to me that would be a job of the security. That's defensive, not offensive. How would you expect the intelligence or against to concentrate on spying the weaknesses in the other -- in the enemy and telling them so that they know how to attack? Am I missing something? Maybe he can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe that would be best in order for me not to provide an explanation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Military Intelligence Service of the Army of Yugoslavia was in charge of setting up its intelligence centres abroad, through which by applying secret methods, so using different technical means they gathered the information that I referred to previously. Secondly, there was also a possibility to legally collect information, because the intelligence administration was a competent body for directing and guiding the work of accredited military representatives of Yugoslavia who worked abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We talked about protection of various plans. Was it a task of a security body to protect plans of the Army of Yugoslavia from being discovered by foreign intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And was it a task of the intelligence body to discover the plans of potential foreign enemies and inform the relevant instances about this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we will take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will invite it in the e-court as a document from 65 ter list of the OTP, 6063. Your Honours, just for your information, and I already discussed this with Mr. Saxon to see how we could resolve this technical problem. So we're talking about rules of service of security organs. This is Exhibit D89, which we tendered through the witness Raseta, but we only tendered some of the articles. Now I will ask this witness to look at some other articles. Mr. Saxon and myself agreed that we might tender this entire document into evidence. It is not so small, not too large either. It has some 40 pages. So once both me and Mr. Saxon are done with all of the articles that we are interested in, it will be up to you to decide whether you want to admit this entire document into evidence or not. So I would like to start now, and then we will see what your decision will be once we -- once we are done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you start, just so that we avoid any confusion and any mistakes, you have called this document by two names. You have called it 65 ter 6063. You've called it D89. You have told us that part of it has already been tendered, part has not been tendered. You're now going to ask this witness to comment on the parts that have not been tendered. Certainly, surely, those parts that have not been tendered could not be part of D89. So I think it's a misnomer to call it D89. Either we're going to look at the new pages and finally agree that they form part of D89 or give them a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also raised this with the secretariat, and I believe it might be best to receive a new exhibit number once I'm finished, and then later on we might put a link between these two exhibits. I believe this might be the best solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's decide that at the time. For now, let us just make it clear on the record that the pages we are going to look at are not part of D89.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this document was written in 1984 and issued by the Federal Secretariat of People's Defence -- or National Defence. Mr. Gajic, as you know, we are interested in the period after the year 1992. So were these rules of service of security organs in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia applied at the time when General Perisic was Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at Article 1. This is on page 5 in B/C/H, and page 6 in English. Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, Article 1 is the one you can see on the screen. Could you please comment what is described here as "The competence of security organs." I will read the second part of paragraph 1. "Security organs as expert organs take -- carry out security tasks as described by the law and regulations adopted pursuant to the law in order to detect and prevent activities aimed at subverting or disrupting the social order established by the constitution and threatening the country's security. If such an activities is carried out in the armed forces or against the armed forces from within the country or from abroad, and also for the purposes of detecting and protecting activities aimed at breaching the secrecy of the plans and preparations for the country's defence." So what was the subject of protection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You indicate that you're going to ask to tender this document. You indicated that it's fairly large. Can we avoid reading it if we are going to tender it? Maybe if the witness can just read it quietly and comment on it rather than you reading it into the record and then later tendering it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're absolutely right. And this is in line with your guidelines. So I will not read it into the transcript. I will just ask the witness to comment on specific articles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic, in this Article 1 what is important here is that security organs as specialist organs of commands, units and institutions of the Army of Yugoslavia are responsible, and this is the key, to protect military forces if such an activity is carried out in the armed forces or against the armed forces from within the country or from abroad. And then secondly, also for the purposes of detecting and preventing activities aimed at breaching the secrecy of the plans and preparations of armed force -- of the armed forces. So this is what matters here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You do not need to read this out, but, rather, comment. I asked you what was the subject of protection of the security organs. Could you answer that in just one sentence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understood this. So they protect the Army of Yugoslavia and its preparations for the country's defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we now see page 6 in B/C/S and page 7 in English, and we will see what were the tasks of the security organs. Articles 6 and 7 of these rules describe the tasks, and they distinguish between two types of activity of the security organs. Article 6 mentions the activities that the security organs are responsible for, and Article 7 describes activities that security organs participate in. Why was this distinction made between these two types of activities of the security organs? So on the one hand, they were responsible for some tasks; and on the other hand, they participated in some other tasks.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, well, if we say that the security organs were responsible for some activities, this means that it was only their responsibility for tasks listed, for example, under item A here, for detection, tracking and preventing the intelligent activities and other activities of foreign military intelligence and so on. So they were responsible. And then all other elements of the command, other secret services, civil secret services, military services, they participated in carrying out these tasks. And in Article 7, if I could please have a look at Article 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second, please. Before we move to the next page, what you just described under (a), was this the key fundamental task that the security organs were responsible for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Under (b) you can also see that they were responsible for the detection and prevention of hostile activities by individuals, groups or organisations against the armed forces. So it is important to point out that we had to discover secret activities. So we were not interested in verbal offences, what was uttered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have a look at the following page, Article 7. If we could just once again mention what the witness emphasised -- or, actually, this is okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 7 consists of several paragraphs describing the tasks in which the security organs participated. You also said this already. So when we are talking about this paragraph (a), why are security organs participating in this activity rather than being responsible for it? Could you tell us that? Could you see it -- can you see it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Mr. Lukic, security organs participated in this because the praxis had shown, when we're talking about this item (a), and this is detection and prevention of serious crimes and so on, most often it was civilians who were involved in such activities, either in an organised fashion or they perpetrated them individually. So it would be different bodies that would be responsible for these tasks, and security organs simply participated in trying to detect, for example, perpetrators of thefts. So they were not responsible for this tasks, but it was the Ministry of the Interior that would be responsible for such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to B/C/S page 8 and English page 9. Item 10. That's the right paragraph, the one that we see in English. The first thing we see on that page is precisely what I'd like the witness to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, this last paragraph in item 10, what exactly do the security organs do in terms of mobilisation plans, plans for the use of the armed forces? What is their share in that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, within this particular field of competence of the security organs, they participate with two documents. One is the assessment of the security situation, and the other is the drafting of a counter-intelligence protection plan in terms of mobilisation plans as an attachment to the mobilisation plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 16, please, B/C/S page 9, English page 10. Article 16. Could you comment on that, sir? This is an article that talks about the chain of command. To put this in the most graphic terms, can you tell us what Article 16 talks about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: I'll try to tackle this by using a specific example. The chief of the security administration of the General Staff of the VJ is directly subordinate to the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ in terms of command and disciplinary responsibility. That is who he answers to for his work, and he is also a member of his collegium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask a question. What does the acronym "NVO" stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, "NVO" stands for "Weapons and military equipment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does Article 18 say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, let me try to give you a specific example of the relations between the army's security organs and the corps' security organs. The army-level security organ, or to be even more specific, the chief of the security department of the army command in a technical sense is superior to the chief of the corps security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we look at this chain of the security organ and they use this term "technical guidance." Why are they not using the term "command"? Can a security organ of a higher command exercise command or merely provide technical guidance? What is the distinction being drawn here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: There is a distinction, Mr. Lukic. That much is true. The first example I talked about was the relationship between the chief of the security administration and the Chief of the General Staff. Chief of the General Staff has certain powers to do with technical guidance on a counter-intelligence basis and he transfers these powers onto the chief of the security administration, meaning the chief of the security administration, as a result of that, can only be in charge of counter-intelligence work of the security organs throughout Yugoslavia, which entails no command responsibility. The only command responsibility is borne by the commander. The principle thus defined is called singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Unity of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next thing we're moving on to is methods of work of the security organ. I want you to comment for me on Article 29, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English reference is page 14, Your Honours; the B/C/S page is 11. The B/C/S spills over into the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does this paragraph tell us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read it, because it actually spills over into the next page. "Security organs are obliged to receive -- security organs are responsible for checking the authenticity of any information received and intelligence and to assess the motives and other facts independent of the sources." When we are talking about anonymous tip-offs they are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't see the rest of the text on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you specifically do in relation to this provision?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, checking or double-checking information intelligence is a fundamental principle applied in the work of security organs. Quite often intelligence or information can be second-hand or misinformation, plain and simple, be it deliberate or not. It is our duty to process all this information that we receive and check the information for authenticity, ideally from a number of different sources. As far as anonymous tip-offs are concerned, or anonymous letters, we only check whenever we believe there is something involved that in legalese might indicate a well-founded suspicion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How exactly does one define these crimes against the armed forces? What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sure. This paragraph -- perhaps we should turn the next page for your benefit, sir. It talks about anonymous tip-offs. It says only those will be checked that indicate the commission of serious crimes against the armed forces. When it says "serious crimes," what exactly does that category entail, just for the benefit of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. For example, the -- there is a terrorist action being planned, an attempt at someone's life, an attempt to break into a military depot in order to steal weapons and military equipment, or any other serious crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is crime a criminal offence against the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the articles in this document that talk about your service specifically, the security administration? Later on we'll say more about how the one over at the General Staff worked. Article 57. The B/C/S page reference is 18, and the English page reference is 23. I will be eliciting your comments on several of these paragraphs. It's quoted here as the SSNO, security administration. I don't think there's any question about that in this courtroom. The security administration when the VJ was established. Let's look at it that way. Where was it, and who was it subordinated to, and later we'll take it from there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the security administration, once the VJ had been established, was one of the independent administrations attached to the General Staff of the VJ and subordinated to the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 57, paragraph 2, is that what we talked about a minute ago, about technical guidance, or as the document states, "Specialist management," as referred to previously in Article 18?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 64, B/C/S page 19, English page 24. Mr. Gajic, can you have a look, please, and comment, if you can, on the specific activities of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, throughout the period of the former Yugoslavia and also once the FRY had been established, we continued to have a degree of co-operation with people from foreign counter-intelligence services and agencies. The co-operation was established pursuant to approval by the Chief of the General Staff and the presidents of the federal organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is reference to the SFRY Presidency in that document. What was the relevant body later on when the constitution had been adopted and provided guidance for your work?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council and the president --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last part of the witness's answer, and could we please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Should I repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Supreme Defence Council -- the approval was granted by the Supreme Defence Council and the president of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to wrap up this document, and I think it might be a good idea to tender the document as a whole and have it received, unless the Chamber believes that we would be better off receiving only particular articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, do you have any comments before we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution concurs with the suggestion of Mr. Lukic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Maybe the best way to do it then is to upload into e-court those parts of Exhibit D9 which -- I beg your pardon, those parts of this document which do not form part of D9 so that D9 becomes a complete document. D89. I beg your pardon. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the course of action that we shall take, but is this about to be given a new number? Oh, no, it isn't. Oh, fine. [In English] Okay. I understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. What about the place of the security administration itself within the general structure of the General Staff? D200 MFI, the order on the respective remits of organisational units. We'll just be looking at the security administration for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the English reference for that is -- translation that got in, that ID 1114D. [In English] Sorry, sorry. Doc ID 11/0333.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic. What's the relationship between D200 MFI and this document that you're mentioning now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D200 is the order on the respective remits of organisational units. You remember we went through that with General Simic and that's why it was MFI'd, because we talked with Mr. Simic about his own organisational unit and with Mr. Nikolic we talked about his organisational unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt? I just want to know whether D200 MFI and ID 11/0333 are one and the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you have in English is a portion of D200 MFI, but you see page 1 in B/C/S, and if you fast forward to Article 24, you will have both the English and the B/C/S in front of you. I'll track the page down for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is -- what is the number of the document you are calling?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D200 MFI --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- [In English] is the exhibit, and the rest is English translation of part of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Let's just call it as D200 MFI and just don't use the other number because it's got to come in both languages if you call it by -- as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 27 in English, if we could see that, please. I'm sorry, this is in -- page reference in Serbian.
