utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, this is the document entitled "Order on organisational units of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia." We will now have a look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could just see the previous page in B/C/S, please. No, the next page. The next page. I'm sorry. Thank you. This is fine. If we could just scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, security administration of the General Staff of the VJ in the period after the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia was established. So there was no more Federal Secretariat, but, rather, the Army of Yugoslavia was set up. So what kind of organisational unit was the security administration at that time? Who was it subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in the period that you mentioned, the security administration was one of the independent administrations of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia directly subordinated to the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And was this true of the entire period from 1994 onwards while General Perisic was Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, in this Article 24, we can see what were the main functions of this administration. There are several listed here, so we can see here counter-intelligence activity. Well, I asked you at the very beginning what was the counter-intelligence activity of the security organs. Can you tell us something about the counter-intelligence activity of the security administration, and let me ask you straight away whether you were at the head of the counter-intelligence department?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you are the right witness to explain this. What was the main task of your department within the security administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the main task of the counter-intelligence department was detection, monitoring of all -- and prevention of all the factors that could threat the Army of Yugoslavia. So any activities of the foreign intelligence and counter-intelligence units, terrorism, or crime. So anything within the Army of Yugoslavia or directed towards the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the following page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the English, please. It's so small.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just find the portion that I would like to read out. Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in, I'm not sure whether this is the correct page in English. It says: "Creates and evaluates analysis and information on intelligence, terrorist and subversive activities carried out within the Army of Yugoslavia or against the Army of Yugoslavia for the needs of security organs."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please see the next page in English so that the Chamber might follow us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see this portion, Mr. Gajic, and could you please comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is paragraph 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic, on the basis of collected intelligence and information, department for analysis of the security administration created different analysis and assessments of such information, and on the basis of this they created certain reports which they submitted to the relevant bodies so that they could make appropriate decisions. At the same time, they would pass this information to the security organs of the Army of Yugoslavia so that they would be informed and so that their activities would be guided in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who would assess and make analysis at the security administration which information would be passed on to the military and state authorities, and which information would be passed on to the lower-level bodies?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the main decision was made by the chief of the security administration on the basis of the proposal made by the chief of the counter-intelligence department, and this was me, and also chief of security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us just say for the sake of the record at the time when Mr. Perisic was Chief of the General Staff, who was the chief of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: During that time chief of security administration was General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic. Could I also provide one additional answer? You asked me who would decide which information would be sent to whom. I need to say that we could also have a different situation when Chief of the General Staff requested some information on certain issues, and even the Supreme Defence Council could request some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now done with this document, so I would kindly ask for this English translation to also be tendered into evidence. So this is D200, but it still needs to be MFI'd because it hasn't been translated entirely yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When we MFI'd this document, it was because it was not translated. Now you are -- you're saying you have an English translation, but you still want it MFI'd because it is not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still do not have the translation of the entire document, Your Honour. The document has some 40 pages. We now provided one portion of the translation, but we still do not have the entire translation. As soon as we have the entire translation ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what does this new translation come under? What number is it you -- D what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you. This is [In English] doc ID 1D11/0333.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's then -- becomes part of D200 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, now we will move from these theoretical considerations to some more practical issues. I would like to learn more about the functioning of the security department -- security administration when we are talking about the internal structure. So there was chief of the security administration. Was there any other body within the security administration? What was its name, and what was its function?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, organisationally speaking, security administration was divided into four departments, and also we had another organisation that was called Counter-intelligence Technical Centre that was directly linked to the security administration. The first department was counter-intelligence department. I was the head of that department, and I think I explained its function. The second department was department of analysis. I believe I also explained its function and its tasks. The third department was military police department, because the security administration was also in charge of professional guidelines of the military police units, provision of equipment for the military police, training the personnel of the military police, and it was only up to the commander to decide on the engagement of the military police. And the fourth department was the logistics department which also encompassed one section that dealt with personnel-related issues. When it comes to the operational and technical centre of the security administration, this was an organisational unit that dealt with application of the counter-intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from these organisational units, was there any other body, so to say, in which representatives of different organisational units met, and how did this body function?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic, for this question. I left this out. So there was a collegium of the chief of the security administration. The collegium was composed of the chiefs of all the departments that I mentioned previously and also the chief of the counter-intelligence operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How often would the collegium meet? Was there any rule?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the collegium of the chief of the security administration met every Monday, most often after -- immediately after the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff. So between noon and 1.00. So these were regular meetings, and if necessary, the collegium could be convened also on additional times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the function of the deputy chief of security administration. Was this a separate position or did somebody hold a different position and in addition was also chief of -- sorry, deputy chief of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: This was a separate position. The deputy chief of the security administration replaced chief of the security administration if the chief was absent, and the counter-intelligence work was obviously the task of the counter-intelligence department and its chief primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would anybody from the security administration participate in the meetings of the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff, and who?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it was chief of the security administration who attended meetings of the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff. Only if the chief was unable to participate in the meetings of the cleanup then it would be his deputy. And if neither the chief nor the deputy could attend those meetings then I would attend them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the security administration have any duty officers or duty teams, and could you explain how this duty service was organised?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The security administration had its duty operative team, the duty operative team of the security administration which consisted of three persons, and they were on duty 24 hours a day. I can also tell you what were their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was my next question. What was their task?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, their task was the following: All the information that they received during a day from the subordinated security organs and all the documents, obviously, they had to compile a daily report on the basis of all of this, which included the most significant security-related data. And that report was then every morning on the following day at 8.00 a.m. be submitted to the chief of the security administration and those of us who were members of his collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that this report was written internally, just for the security administration purposes, or was it drafted for somebody else?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this was an internal document of the security administration, but we also made an extract from that report. That extract consisted of some six to seven sentences, not more, and that extract was taken to the General Staff operations centre, and there there was also a duty operative team and a representative of the security body within that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what I wanted to clarify now. We already heard some testimonies concerning the duty operative team of the General Staff, so could you please tell us, what was the relation between the General Staff duty operative team and the security administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the duty operative team at the operations centre was formed pursuant to an order of the General Staff, and the order also specifies the persons that participated in that duty operative team, and among them was also a representative of the security administration. The duty operative team met every evening at about 9.00 p.m. Most often I was the person that attended the meetings of the duty operative team, and I carried with me that extract, those six or seven sentences containing the most relevant data on what had happened in the previous 24 hours. So they were representatives of all the different sectors, all administrations, and we would read out those short reports and discuss them, reports concerning different areas of responsibility. And after our discussions, we would define what would be entered into the document of the duty operative team, and that report would be submitted in the morning to the Chief of General Staff and members of his collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the security administration, in addition to these daily reports, submit any other reports to the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the security administration submitted to the Chief of General Staff and members of the Supreme Defence Council on a regular basis monthly information, and these monthly information included data on the most significant events and problems during -- that occurred during the previous months. In addition, the security administration also drafted the so-called problem-related information sheets for the Chief of General Staff and sometimes also for members of the Supreme Defence Council. I will mention some examples. For example, if we had a large-scale theft of weapons and the perpetrators were unknown, a team of security personnel would be engaged in trying to detect the perpetrators. So if we discovered who the perpetrators were, on the basis of all of our actions and information collected, we would compile an information sheet and inform the Chief of the General Staff about this. So how come that this could happen? What were the problems, the breaches in the security? Who were the participants in this crime, whether any military personnel participated and we would also propose certain measures. And obviously it would be up to the chief to decide on such measures. Thirdly, if I may, there were quite many demands by the Chief of the General Staff for assessments to be forwarded, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The monthly report that you defined as a regular report forwarded to the Chief of General Staff and the Supreme Defence Council, is that the same sort of report that is then dispatched to both these addresses or are two separate reports drafted for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there was just a single difference between the two. In the report to the Chief of the General Staff and the president of the Supreme Defence Council, there was a section covering the military police. Other than that, they were identical in terms of substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have told us no difference, sir. Your answer says: "There was just a single difference between the two. In the report to the Chief of the General Staff and the president of the Supreme Defence Council, there was a section covering the military police. Other than that, they were identical in terms of substance." So they seem to be identical all the way through. There's no -- you haven't shown any difference at all. You've told us that the two that go to the two authorities cover military police. Can you give the answer again and try to tell us what the difference is between the report that goes to the Chief of the General Staff and the president of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the monthly report sent to the Chief of the General Staff and the president of the Supreme Defence Council, there were two components; the counter-intelligence component and the military police involvement component. As for the -- all the other members of the Supreme Defence Council, no information on the military police involvement was included, that being the only difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this might be a good time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed. We will take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we spoke about those meetings and the security administration, the collegium, the duty operations team, information like that. In addition to what we have been discussing, were there any daily meetings that were being held by certain individuals in the security administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there were indeed daily meetings being held, attended by the chief security administration, by me, and sometimes the deputy chief. These took place each morning. We would drink coffee and then go on to analyse the daily operative reports that I referred to earlier on. At these normally brief meetings, the chief of the security administration would hand out assignments if there were any to distribute, after which we would try and reach an agreement on what we would be doing over the course of that day. At the end of each day, meaning sometime past 2000 hours, we would meet again to analyse what we could achieve in terms of covering the assignments discussed that same morning, and to see whether there were any tasks we were facing for the following day. We discussed a number of other issues of present concern as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to move on to something entirely different. Mr. Gajic, what about your involvement and that of the security administration? Did you know anything about information suggesting there were undercover secret campaigns of people arming themselves prior to 1990? Who exactly -- prior to the break-up of the country, who exactly was arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. Lukic. I was with the security administration of the team. The chief of the security administration was General Aleksandar Vasiljevic. We monitored this, and we tried to uncover any attempts to obtain illegal weapons. Even throughout the former Yugoslavia that was one of the points on which the security administration focused. It was quite difficult to monitor these difficulties in what used to be the Republic of Croatia and then in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, and to some extent, I suppose, also Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What sort of information did you manage to obtain?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we came across information that throughout the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina there were two large-scale paramilitary formations being established. In Croatia's case this was the National Guards Corps. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Patriotic League of Nations, or the National Patriotic League, and this was something that was done pursuant to decisions taken by the republican leaderships, Dr. Tudjman in Croatia and Alija Izetbegovic in Bosnia-Herzegovina. These paramilitary formations were now to be armed. They were first established in order to enter into armed clashes with the then-JNA for purposes of breaking away. We monitored these illegal arming activities throughout 1990, and particularly in 1991, we managed to uncover about nine large-scale illegal channels through which these weapons were arriving. Six of these had to do with Croatia, two having to do with Bosnia and Herzegovina, and a single one was, in fact, in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Having obtained that kind of information, what exactly did you do? What steps did you take, and what did that lead to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in Croatia's case, we staged an operation that was conducted by General Vasiljevic as chief of the administration personally. The operation was called Operation Shield. During this, we obtained incontrovertible material evidence of illegal weapons coming in. What one needed to do was arrest the perpetrators but there was a political decision that was taken not to do that, to abstain from arresting those people. This in turn led to the outbreak of war in Croatia back in 1991 and Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Operation Shield, you say. Was that the operation that involved Spegelj, and was the public duly informed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was also known as Operation Spegelj, and the public was duly informed, as well as both the military and political leaderships. There was detailed information provided on that as well as some footage that was shown to the general public in Yugoslavia and abroad demonstrating that Croatia was preparing for war and obtaining weapons, although the Security Council Resolutions clearly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honours. I've let this gone on for a while but I must ask my colleague, please, if he can explain what is the relevance of this evidence to the issues of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During this trial the Prosecution has brought up a lot of evidence about the period preceding the eruption of armed conflicts, situations having to do with illegal weapons being brought in, and they talked about the situation before 1992, the existence of local Territorial Defence units and generally all of the three ethnic groups arming themselves. I think this is relevant primarily in order to demonstrate how the three armies came about, or even six or seven armies, how they came about. I think this has a direct bearing on some counts in the indictment, especially the criminal responsibility of Mr. Perisic in terms of aiding and abetting. Then, on the other hand, this has to do with the events that preceded the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll allow the question to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I won't press the point any further, but I am going to address the general period. Can you put us in the right frame, generally speaking. Operation Shield, when was its cover blown?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Sometime in late 1991 or perhaps early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, do you have any direct personal knowledge or professional second-hand knowledge about the situations of the members of the offices of the JNA in the then still -- the unified and single Yugoslavia back in 1991 and 1992 in the individual republics?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the situation throughout Yugoslavia, both in a political and military sense, was quite complex and complicated. If we look at the situation of the JNA officers, both proper officers and NCOs, the worst place for them to be was Croatia. They were facing a lot of propaganda pressure and even open threats that sometimes went as far as people being evicted from their flats. Their wives were being fired from their jobs, and mixed marriages were under particular pressure, for example, in cases where you had a Serbian husband and a Croat wife. The wives would get lots of pressure to get a divorce, to divorce from these Chetnik officers. That was the going phrase at the time. Their children were mistreated in kindergarten, school, elementary schools, secondary schools, universities. Many of them no longer even dared go to school and the children would, for that reason, remain at home. People were being harassed by telephone, in their homes. Normally this type of harassment would occur sometime between midnight and 4.00 in the morning, and the messages being put across were to the effect of "Go away. Run back to Serbia. We'll kill you. We'll cut your throat," and suchlike.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you get this information, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I have personal experience of this. It was pursuant to an order by the chief of the security administration, General Vasiljevic, that I spent the period between the 1st and 7th of July 1991 in Croatia in order to carry out an inspection. In fact, I visited or toured six or seven different garrisons where brigade-level units were stationed. I spoke directly to officers belonging to -- to all the different ethnic groups. Not just the Serbs there but also the Croats, the Muslims, and everyone else. They confirmed this and also shared with me a number of other even more serious incidents, but our time is short and I'm not pressing this any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did cases such as these occur in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, this type of thing emerged at a somewhat later date. I was chief of security until October 1990, and you can say that things were relatively quiet at this time. It wasn't before late 1990, when the people's Patriotic League was established as a paramilitary formation, that the first symptoms started to crop up as they had previously in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the period while Yugoslavia still existed? Let's talk about 1990 and all the way up until late 1991. Were there any attacks on the barracks in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, JNA military installations? What exactly was happening?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, at the time you specified, in Croatia most of the barracks were under siege or being blocked by paramilitaries. Therefore, the communication between officers was quite limited. They had to be protected by armed escorts because it was too risky for them to leave those compounds on their own. Secondly, sometimes their electricity and water supplies would be cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was doing this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: The local authorities for the most part, the newly established ones. The extremists had now come to power, for the most part belonging to the leading political party. I'm talking the most extremist faction of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who was it that was having their electricity and water supplies cut off?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: The barracks, the officers and the soldiers there. What is particularly noteworthy, if I may add, is that combat-readiness measures had been raised already by this time. Therefore, the officers and soldiers would spend all their lives around the clock in these barracks. Now, imagine what their situation must have been given the fact that they had no electricity or water in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you have any direct knowledge of any developments in April 1992 regarding the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I was back with the security administration by this time. I had been transferred from the 1st Army back to the security administration. We had an operations duty team, and we received information and some documents to the effect that a clash was in the offing with the army. Their leadership was behind this, and the former JNA Territorial Defence had been now transformed into their own Territorial Defence. The People's Patriotic League was also readying for clashes with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume you misspoke when you said the former JNA Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence in the old system, what was it part of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: The armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a 65 ter document from the Defence list, 65 ter 00381D. I have a binder here, as a matter of fact, which I forgot to hand over to the witness. Maybe it might be easier for the witness to consult. So he might as well keep it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see this document on the screen, Mr. Gajic, before you receive the paper version? Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is a decision on the withdrawal of JNA units from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated 27 April 1992, decision adopted by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and signed by Alija Izetbegovic. First of all, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I already saw this document on the 27th of April, when it was adopted, because the chief of the security, Colonel Bjelosevic, who was the staff of the Territorial Defence, he was replaced when the new authorities came. However, he kept some of his competencies and he sent this document to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "us"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: To the security administration. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under the II, can you please read what it says and comment on it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in the first paragraph of Article II, members of the JNA are invited, those that were in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and to, Herzegovina join the newly formed forces of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to place themselves at their disposal. And in the second paragraph, it is stated that those members of the JNA who did not wish to place themselves at their disposals shall have all their rights guaranteed and that no actions would be taken against them or members of their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information as to whether JNA officers who joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether they received any salaries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the largest number of those who joined the Territorial Defence were people of Muslim nationality, and some of them were also of Croatian nationality. As far as I know, their -- they took it upon themselves to pay out their salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article III is rather clear. I would like to take a look at VI and VII. Could you read those and tell us what was your impression of this entire document when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the following page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic, if you allow me, I will comment on Article VI first of all. If you look at the contents of this article, you can see that it is politically correct, so to say, but this was written for the sake of the general public. In the field, however, the situation went in a rather opposite direction. So what we knew at our security administration at the time was that conflict and even an armed conflict was imminent. And Article VII is linked to Article VI, and it explains that all the problems will be resolved between authorised organs of the former JNA and the state organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D262. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see on the screen Exhibit D00381. I apologise. We already saw that one. Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please see the document from the Defence 65 ter list, 00377D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, have you seen this document? This is a document -- this is the document of the Ministry for People's Defence, Territorial Defence Staff, signed by Mr. Hasan Efendic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you see it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: We received it in the same way in which we received the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please read item 1, and could you please comment. So what was your impression of this document once you received it in your administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, item 1 says that a complete and full-scale blockade of all roads in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was to be carried out. So wherever units of the former JNA have begun to pull out materiel and technical equipment, and this had to be done in direct co-ordination with the Ministry of the Interior. When we received this document, this entire document, you're now only asking about item 1, there was no reason whatsoever to issue an order of this kind, because the Yugoslav Army in the two days between the 27th of April when the Presidency made its decision and the 29th of April did not make any step which would call for an order of this kind. And if I may add, because I was at the security administration at the time, I know that the representative of the federal secretary for defence, Mr. Adzic at the time, was engaged in exchange of letters with Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and these letters had to do with an attempt to resolve issues in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the political level and for the JNA to act in accordance with whatever political solution was decided on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In item 3, we can see that it was requested to prevent unannounced leaving of JNA units from their barracks without the escort of the MUP. So did you know that there were attempts made by JNA units to pull out of their barracks in an unorganised manner?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as far as I knew, the bulk of the activities at the time had to do with logistical issues, so supplying them with food and other materials necessary. There were no large-scale movements that would call for an order of this type.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the introduction to this order, it is mentioned that the property of the Bosnia and Herzegovina started to be plundered by the former JNA members. Were you informed about any such activities by JNA members in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we had no such information, and I believe that they simply needed an excuse for war or for a conflict. They simply needed an excuse for -- to start a conflict with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you are saying "they," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Territorial Defence, paramilitaries, and their leadership who was informed about all of this, at least some members of the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask this document to be tendered into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D263. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, do you know whether there were any incidents in Sarajevo and, if so, what really happened there after the 29th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Sadly, I do know about this, Mr. Lukic. There was an attack of -- by a paramilitary unit called Green Berets against the building of the JNA in Sarajevo. On that occasion, the chief of the JNA home, who was a Macedonian, was gravely injured. He later died of these injuries. And several soldiers were also injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: This was on the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, your question was what happened on the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I asked after the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic, once the JNA building was attacked, the command decided to send a unit there to provide assistance to the officers and soldiers who were there. However, they were attacked by the paramilitaries, and again several persons were injured. Quite a few of them, as far as I remember. Nobody was killed, but there were many injured persons, and a lot of equipment was destroyed. Then a unit was sent from the police [as interpreted], but that one also did not manage to get to the JNA building because it was also encountered by paramilitary members who destroyed some of the equipment and again injured some of the soldiers. And on -- at that point, the idea of any further action was given up on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any new attacks in the days to come, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: In the following days, Mr. Lukic, the command of the 2nd Military Zone was attacked. So these are four buildings. And inside these buildings there was a number of soldiers and civilians. That attack was launched at about noon, and it lasted until 10.00 p.m. During this attack, all the four buildings were badly damaged. The equipment was plundered and members of the JNA were injured during the attack. On the 2nd of May, we had the gravest incident --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second, please. Allow me not to forget this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 68, line 10, the witness actually said "military police." It was a military police unit that was sent to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please continue, sir. So what happened on the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, on the 2nd of May, president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, came back from Lisbon where he attended negotiations on a plan for Bosnia and Herzegovina. He landed at Butmir Airport in Sarajevo, and nearby there was a command of the 4th Corps of the JNA, and one part of the command of the 2nd Military Zone were also there with commander, Mr. Kukanjac. The commander made an estimate of the situation. General MacKenzie was also there, who was in charge of the international peace forces in Sarajevo for Bosnia and Herzegovina. So they made an estimate of the situation, and they said that if they would allow Mr. Izetbegovic to go on his own or escorted by members of his MUP, probably he would be killed and probably JNA would be blamed for that. So they suggested to Mr. Izetbegovic to be escorted by members of the military and with MacKenzie and several vehicles from his units. So there was a column of some 30 vehicles with many officers, soldiers, and a lot of military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose vehicles were they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, these were military vehicles in which there was Mr. Alija Izetbegovic; commander of the 2nd Military Zone, General Kukanjac; and also General MacKenzie, as commander of the international forces that were present in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They went towards the Presidency building of Bosnia-Herzegovina because they wanted to escort Mr. Izetbegovic there safely. In Dobrovoljacka Street in Sarajevo, which is a very narrow street in Sarajevo which prevents any manoeuvre of the vehicles, that convoy was stopped by paramilitary forces who made a massacre there. I'm not sure how many people were killed, how many soldiers, and how many were injured, both soldiers and officers. Vehicles were set on fire. They were plundered, and as far as I remember, over 100 soldiers and officers were detained. As far as I remember, General MacKenzie and Colonel Koljevic drove back to see what happened, but they were turned away. He later told General Kukanjac that what he had seen there was a scene of utmost horror, the likes of which he had never witnessed in his military career, such acts of cruelty being perpetrated against soldiers, officers, NCOs, and civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think we must try and supervise the testimony as it goes out. You asked a very short, simple question, "Whose vehicles were these?" We've heard a long answer, and that question has not been answered. We really need to -- we -- your question was very simple. "Whose vehicles were they," and we've got a quarter page of answer which doesn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness was answering something that I would have asked him at any rate later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He mustn't anticipate your questions. He must answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, that was the reason I asked the question. Whose column was it that you described?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: The column of the 2nd military district. It was a military column.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you've said that already. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JNA, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. So the JNA was protecting Izetbegovic and MacKenzie?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have a 65 ter Defence document, 65 ter 01011D. [In English] 01011D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this document, I just want to get some clarity. You said the JNA was protecting President Izetbegovic and MacKenzie. Now, who were attacking this column that was protecting them? You said that MacKenzie said he witnessed a massacre like he had never seen before. Who perpetrated this massacre in that narrow street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the massacre was perpetrated by a paramilitary Muslim formation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, is it the testimony that a Muslim paramilitary formation which had been established by Izetbegovic's order was attacking a column that was protecting Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A while ago you said there were assessments to the effect that someone might try to kill Izetbegovic after his return from Lisbon. That's what you said. Whose assessments were those, and whose interests would have been served that scenario?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Alija Izetbegovic was an extremist. That much can be said. Nevertheless, he was far more realistic than some other people who were with him and were part of the leadership. The most extremist among them being Ejup Ganic. Based on such intelligence as we gathered at the time, as well as evidence, in fact, in relation to the Dobrovoljacka Street massacre and everything else that I've been talking about, Ejup Ganic is a person who bears direct responsibility for that, if I may put it that way. He was in charge of the entire operation. I understand your question. When we talk about any danger to Alija Izetbegovic's life or the possibility that he might be killed, the people I had in mind were Ejup Ganic and his own extremist faction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I need to understand, because you see at page 72, starting from line 5, Mr. Gajic, you say: "Mr. Lukic, Alija Izetbegovic was an extremist. That much can be said. Nevertheless, he was far more realistic than some other people who were with him and were part of the leadership. The most extremist among them being Ejup Ganic." Now, if Ejup Ganic was with him, what prevented him from killing him if that's what he wanted to do? If you're saying he was the one masterminding this attack. You see, I've got several questions here. Here's a person who is with Izetbegovic, but he's at the same time masterminding the attack that is attacking Izetbegovic, and he's part of Izetbegovic's leadership. Can you unravel that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the situation within the Muslim leadership was quite complex and -- yes, complex. In the formal sense, they were united in the sense of rallying around a goal that they shared, an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nevertheless, each of them separately had their own goals and objectives in terms of struggling to attain power for themselves. Ejup Ganic was peculiar because he believed that this should be achieved by the use of armed force. Alija Izetbegovic was, in a way, more moderate in this sense. He was advocating talks and was in favour of seeking a political solution. He was more realistic and more moderate; Ejup Ganic and his own faction were not happy with that. There were smouldering tensions between them that at times became more apparent than at other times. Nevertheless, they, too, were perfectly aware of the fact that there was a threat of open clashes breaking out between them, even severe ones. I do apologise, Your Honour. I have to add one thing. What I said in relation to Ejup Ganic, it was subsequent inquiries and investigations that showed up their relationship for what it was, indicating also that Ejup Ganic was prepared to go as far as to physically liquidate Alija Izetbegovic. And then the events eventually took the course they did later on in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, but what I do not understand is how he is actually with, physically with, Izetbegovic and part of his leadership and at the same time masterminding an attack against him. And added to that, that in fact this whole convoy is being given protection by the JNA who are being attacked by the very paramilitary formed by -- military force from -- by the very people they are protecting. The order by -- it just doesn't make -- and I understand that you say it's complex, but it just doesn't sort of settle well in my mind how these things happen, how enemies are in bed together and friends kill one another.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will do my best to answer. I'm not sure if I was specific enough previously. Ejup Ganic was not part of the same convoy as General MacKenzie. That's one thing. Secondly, if I may refer to history. We have often seen that kind of principle at work, the closest of associates turning one another's murderers, assassinating a head of state, for example, although previously they might have worked together. This may perhaps be somewhat difficult to understand, but it depicts faithfully the complex nature of the situation that prevailed in Bosnia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gajic. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't be dwelling on this with Mr. Gajic, not on this particular episode, and I do believe the document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the document that we have on our screens right now, a report on the 4th Corps command, dated the 7th of May, 1992, signed by Milutin Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, please, what is it about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: This is a report by commander of the 2nd Military District on developments throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. It also comments on the way in which those developments politically affected the JNA. The JNA at the time still being based throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there a description of the Dobrovoljacka Street massacre in this report, or the incident there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, as well as all the other developments that I have been referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document please be received, Your Honours. I believe it is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D264. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence 65 ter 00641D. Can that be brought up, please. The heading reads, "A list of wounded JNA members," the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I showed you this document during proofing, sir, didn't I? General, let me ask you this: Do you actually know any of these persons whose names we can see listed here, as briefly as possible?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I do know a number of the persons listed here. Number 1, Enes Taso, colonel, an ethnic Muslim who was wounded during the attack on Dobrovoljacka Street. Number 3, Ratko Katalina, colonel, chief of security of the 2nd Military District. Severely wounded. Remaining handicapped for life. He now lives in Belgrade, as does Enes Taso. Both retired with the rank of colonel. Number 5, Blagoje Bozinovski, lieutenant-colonel, a Macedonian by ethnicity. A person I mentioned earlier on. He had been wounded at the JNA hall, eventually succumbing to his injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be received, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is received. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D265. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last document in relation to our present topic, Defence 65 ter 00653D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a list containing the names of 122 persons who the document claims were captured on the 2nd and 3rd of May in Sarajevo. Any familiar names, sir? Any details concerning their fate in Sarajevo on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I am familiar with some of these names. Number 1, Slavoljub Belosevic, colonel, chief of security. The republican staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina's TO. He was captured and badly mistreated for the subsequent ten days by a group of Green Berets. He was eventually set free. Number 7, Milan Suput, colonel. Commander of a military police battalion, the very battalion that I spoke of, in fact. When they offered relief to the JNA hall after it had been attacked, he was captured and subsequently released. Number 33, Franjo Patacko, a lieutenant-colonel, a Croat, who was also captured and eventually released.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be received, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D266. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know how many persons were killed on that occasion, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I couldn't give you the exact figure. Nevertheless, speaking of professional soldiers, between six and seven were killed. Two or three civilians as well, women, I think. What we don't see on the list is the number of dead, but there is one person who was killed whom I wish to mention specially, Colonel Bosko Mihajlovic who was chief of security in the republican staff of the TO in Zagreb, Croatia. Following the withdrawal of the JNA, he was transferred to Sarajevo. The only reason he was killed was because he told the Green Berets killing all the people there, "Why on earth are you mistreating us, mistreating us? Just let us go," whereupon they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a similar incident that occurred elsewhere after this one, and what were the consequences of that other incident? Briefly if you can, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will just mention Tuzla. Did anything like that happen there as well, and what exactly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Thanks for jogging my memory, Mr. Lukic. Yes, indeed, there was something that happened. In 1991, the first embryo of the People's Patriotic League was created in Tuzla. One of the founding members was Vahid Karavelic. I knew him personally, and he held the rank of captain at the time. He's directly responsible for the killing of an officer as --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me specifically about the Tuzla incident and the attack on that column in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: We're talking about an incident in which a column was attacked heading out of Bosanska Buna barracks and on its way to Brcanska Malta. About 200 soldiers and officers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was it approximately?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this was also in 1992, possibly 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will now move to an entirely different topic. Before this Court we have heard testimonies to the effect that in May 1992, after the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted, the law on the new army, the Army of Yugoslavia, was also adopted. We also know that the Republika Srpska was formed as a state, and so was the Republika Srpska Krajina, and they had their respective armies. What was the relationship, if any, of the security organs of these three armies?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, these were three entirely separated security organs. They were separated and independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to hear whether in your mind these were three separate armies.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, three entirely separate and independent armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was the foundation for the establishment of these three armies? What was the legal framework on the basis of which they were established?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, these armies were based pursuant to the constitution and different pieces of legislation, Law on Defence and Law on the Army, passed by the highest legislative bodies. So the assemblies, the parliaments of these states, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I will ask about the relationships between security bodies. So what was your relationship, the relationship of the security administration and you personally, with security organs of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Those relations were based on some ad hoc contacts and exchange of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you possibly explain what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: So we had no formal relations. We had no laws or other regulations that would govern our relations, but, rather, those relations were based on our personal assessment and on the needs for exchange of information. We would come in contacts -- the representatives of our security administration and security bodies of these two republics would come into contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A short while ago you explained security organs, security administration, intelligence administration. Do you know how these professional structures were set up in Republika Srpska or in the Republic of Srpska Krajina? Did they also have two separate administrations or did they have a different system?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in the Serbian Army of Krajina, they had a security department with a chief who was directly subordinated to the chief of Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina. In the Army of Republika Srpska, they had a security intelligence sector, and the chief of that sector was subordinated to the chief of Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This intelligence security sector, did it encompass both security organs and intelligence organs or was it just its name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Lukic. The chief of intelligence security sector was superior of the chief of intelligence department and the chief of security department of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the chief of the security department of the Serbian Army of Krajina, first of all, and did you know that person yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there were several chiefs of security department, Colonel Dusan Smiljanic, also Colonel Vuk Dimitrovic, and Colonel Rade Raseta. I knew all these three officers in person since they used to be members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were they previously involved with the security tasks in the JNA? Is that how you knew them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in the Army of Republika Srpska, do you know who was the head of the intelligence security sector and who was in charge of the security issues?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the head of the intelligence -- or, rather, chief of intelligence security sector was colonel and later General Zdravko Tolimir, and Mr. Ljubisa Beara was chief of the military security, and the chief of military intelligence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's apology. We did not catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Colonel Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked whether you knew these persons.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I knew them. Colonel Tolimir and later General Tolimir, Zdravko, and Captain Ljubisa Beara were in the security organs of the former JNA, and Colonel Salapura was in the intelligence organs of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I asked you at the beginning where were you born, and you told us that you were born in Croatia. Now I would like to ask you whether anybody ever requested that you join the Serbian Army of Krajina. So during the period after that army was formed whilst you were in the security administration.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, to answer the first part of your question, I need to say no; and concerning the second part of your question, I can say that I requested myself on two occasions to join the Serbian Army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? Did you simply want to visit them, or did you want to become a member of the Serbian Army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: My aim was to become a member of the Serbian Army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened? Why didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the first time I requested it, it was in 1993, when I was chief of security in the 1st Army, and the then commander of the army, General Stojanovic, did not allow me to go. He told me that I was needed there as chief of security of the 1st Army. The second time I requested to go to the Serbian Army of Krajina and become its member was in early April of 1994, when I was transferred back to the security administration. The then chief of the security administration, General Dimitrijevic, also told me that I couldn't go because they needed me there, and he told me that he already agreed on this with Chief of the General Staff, General Perisic, who also believed that I should have stayed at the security administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gajic, on -- on the question when we were -- you were asked, in particular, whether you had applied to join the Serbian Army in Krajina, you said that you asked on two occasions and on two occasions that was refused. So my question is the following: Why did you not resign from the Yugoslav Army to -- to join the Serbian army in Krajina, in Croatia? I mean, it seemed to me that that would have been the simplest thing to do if you wanted to serve in the Serbian Army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was needed in the Army of Yugoslavia, so I thought it would be a dishonourable thing to do to turn my back to the Army of Yugoslavia, which needed me. Somebody estimated that they needed me there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, do you know whether in the security administration or within the General Staff, were there any other people who were born in Croatia or Bosnia and who also did not go and join other armies? Did you know of any such persons?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any of them suffered any consequences because they didn't leave and join these other armies, any consequences in terms of their promotions, their careers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, nobody suffered any consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you name any of your colleagues who was there and who shared similar roots as you did and who stayed within the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I can mention two or three names now. First of all, Colonel Novakovic, Marko, or -- who was born in Bosnia and Herzegovina, who was in the security organs at the Ministry of Defence. Also, Colonel Svilar who was in the Counter-Intelligence Technical Centre that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just repeat that name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Colonel Svilar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to that Colonel Svilar? What was his origin?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Colonel Svilar was born in the Republic of Srpska Krajina. He held -- had some health problems, and everybody originating from the Republic of Srpska Krajina was interviewed, and they were all asked whether they wanted to join these armies so that they could be dispatched there. And such an interview was also held with Colonel Svilar, and he said that he had some serious health-related issues and that he also couldn't do it because of his family. So as far as I know, he remained at the same position and he retired from that position eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he suffer from any consequences because he didn't agree to being dispatched? Did he retire regularly or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I retired on 31st of December, 2001. As far as I know, Colonel Svilar retired one year after me, and this was his regular time for retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we are right on time to finish for today, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The case is going to stand postponed to tomorrow in the afternoon at quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom II. You are warned, sir, while you are still in the witness stand you may not discuss the case with anybody, not even with your lawyers. Thank you so much. Back here at quarter past 2.00, tomorrow afternoon. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of March, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
